title: The changed business: Napster, streaming royalties and remote record-making
summary: He says the business changed after 2000, streaming pays little, and records are now built by sending files rather than playing together.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: What would get you back into the studio now as a producer?

It would have to be an old friend wanting me to do something with them again. Because if it was a new artist now, honestly I wouldn’t know what to do — I mean I’d know what to do musically but I wouldn’t know what to do because the structure, the business has changed so dramatically since 2000, the year 2000. Particularly. I look at that as the watershed year because that’s when the kids came out with Napster and people were downloading music and the income just — they’re talking about now how streaming has lifted up the record companies, but I still get my statements. And it’s like for a stream I’m looking at .0002 cents, you know? That type of thing. Whereas it used to be eight dollars and something from this, that and the other. The royalties I make now are still from the old records, because the new stuff that’s streamed — I just read an article talking about how streaming has lifted the record industry back up, but nobody hardly buys physical product anymore. There’s almost as much vinyl sold now as there are CDs because that’s come back. But compared to — most of it’s streamed. And first of all, I don’t like the

sound of streamed music because of the compression that’s necessary. I don’t care for the way records are made in the most part. One of the students was asking me during the fire drill up here, how records are made. I said, “Well you know I know all the great players that are still around, but they rarely are called in to do live sessions anymore. The way it’s done mostly now, with the exception of jazz and bluegrass and classical, a producer and his artist lay down a drum loop and maybe an acoustic guitar or a piano. They send it to Eddie Bayer’s, my longtime friend and drummer. They send it to Eddie, he puts down his part in his own studio. Then it goes back up to a dropbox, iCloud, whatever. Then Michael Rhodes the bass player gets it and adds his part. Back up. Then it goes to whoever, Matt Rawlings to add piano. They hardly ever see each other in the studio anymore. And the magic was out on the floor what happened. Here’s your chart. But then there’s that magic, that give and take. Hey what about this? What about this little lick right here? What about this? And that’s the magic. Doing records like this, emailing them to each other or whatever, you don’t get that interaction. And the guys tell me that. They are seldom called into a session anymore where they’re all there. Because this is the way it’s done. And I said unfortunately to me that’s the way the records sound. I started hearing it oh way back. I called it homogenization. Because they were all mixed exactly the same, they tried to get the loudest level they could for radio at that time, and then it was like they’d have to be compressed tremendously to be streamed and kids listen in the earbuds. It’s not the full sonic spectrum anymore in those records. Now again I’m sure somebody will look at this and it’s just some old guy talking about the way it used to be. I’m not bitter about it, I got to do it at the right time. We all said how lucky we were. It was the best of those old guys that we got to learn from. Not just the horn players and the string players but the great old rhythm sections like the Wrecking Crew in L.A. or the Funk Brothers in Detroit. We got to learn from them and kind of take the baton through our period. And then it just started drifting away after our era. So I’m not bitter about it. I’m grateful that I did it when I did it.
